myths.claim: Goldfish have a 3-second memory
myths.receipt: Lab goldfish have been trained to push levers for food and respond to feeding sounds, and they remember those tricks for months, not seconds.

myths.claim: We only use 10% of our brain
myths.receipt: Brain scans show activity across virtually every region over a day, and damage to almost any area causes problems. There is no idle 90%.

myths.claim: The Great Wall of China is visible from space with the naked eye
myths.receipt: It is only a few metres wide and the same colour as the land around it. Astronauts, including China's first astronaut Yang Liwei, said they couldn't see it.

myths.claim: Bulls hate the colour red
myths.receipt: Bulls are red-green colour blind. They charge at the cape because it moves, not because it is red.

myths.claim: Lightning never strikes the same place twice
myths.receipt: The Empire State Building gets hit around 20 to 25 times a year. Tall pointy things get struck again and again.

myths.claim: Hair and nails keep growing after you die
myths.receipt: The skin dries out and pulls back after death, which makes hair and nails look longer. Nothing is actually growing.

myths.claim: Cracking your knuckles gives you arthritis
myths.receipt: Dr Donald Unger cracked the knuckles on only one hand for over 60 years and found no arthritis difference between his hands. He won an Ig Nobel Prize for it. Studies agree: no link found.

myths.claim: Bats are blind
myths.receipt: No bat species is blind. Many see well, and lots of them use echolocation on top of their eyesight.

myths.claim: Napoleon was super short
myths.receipt: He was about 1.69 metres, around 5 foot 7, average or a bit above for a Frenchman of his time. The myth comes from old French inches and British cartoon propaganda.

myths.claim: Vikings wore horned helmets
myths.receipt: There is no evidence Viking warriors wore horned helmets. The look was popularised by costume designs for Wagner's opera in 1876.

myths.claim: Carrots give you night vision
myths.receipt: During World War Two the British spread this story to hide that their pilots were using radar. Vitamin A helps normal eyesight, but extra carrots won't give you night vision.

myths.claim: Sugar makes kids hyperactive
myths.receipt: Double-blind studies found no difference in behaviour between kids given sugar and kids given a placebo. Parents who believed their kid had sugar rated them as more hyper anyway.

myths.claim: Shaving makes hair grow back thicker
myths.receipt: Shaving cuts hair at a blunt angle so the stubble feels coarse, but studies going back to 1928 show it doesn't change thickness, colour or growth rate.

myths.claim: You swallow 8 spiders a year in your sleep
myths.receipt: There is no study behind that number. A sleeping human is a noisy, breathing, vibrating giant, which spiders avoid.

myths.claim: Chameleons change colour to blend in
myths.receipt: They mostly change colour to signal mood and to control temperature, by rearranging tiny crystals in their skin.

myths.claim: Ostriches bury their heads in the sand
myths.receipt: They don't. They lower their heads to turn their eggs in ground nests, or lie flat to hide, which from far away looks like a buried head.

myths.claim: If you touch a baby bird its mother will reject it
myths.receipt: Most birds have a weak sense of smell and don't abandon chicks because a human touched them. Still, best to leave wildlife alone.

myths.claim: Different parts of your tongue taste different flavours
myths.receipt: Every taste zone can detect every basic taste. The famous tongue map came from a misread translation of a 1901 German paper.

myths.claim: Dogs only see in black and white
myths.receipt: Dogs see colour, just fewer of them. They have two types of colour cones and mostly see blues and yellows.

myths.claim: Humans only have five senses
myths.receipt: You also have balance, a sense of where your body is, temperature, pain and more. Scientists count way more than five.

myths.claim: Your blood is blue until it touches air
myths.receipt: Blood is always red: darker red in veins, brighter in arteries. Veins look blue because of how light passes through skin.

myths.claim: A penny dropped from a skyscraper can kill someone
myths.receipt: A penny is flat and light, so air resistance caps its speed at roughly 40 to 80 km per hour. It would sting, not kill.

myths.claim: Mount Everest is the tallest mountain on Earth
myths.receipt: Everest has the highest peak above sea level. Measured from base to peak, Mauna Kea in Hawaii is taller, over 10,000 metres, most of it underwater.

myths.claim: Food on the floor is fine if you grab it within 5 seconds
myths.receipt: A Rutgers study found bacteria can transfer to food in under one second. Wet food picks up more, faster.

myths.claim: Alcohol warms you up when it's cold
myths.receipt: Alcohol widens blood vessels near your skin, so you feel warm while your core actually loses heat faster.

myths.claim: You must wait 30 minutes after eating to swim
myths.receipt: There's no evidence that swimming after a meal causes dangerous cramps or drowning. Safety groups have found no documented cases.

myths.claim: People in the Middle Ages thought the Earth was flat
myths.receipt: Educated Europeans knew the Earth was round. The ancient Greek Eratosthenes even estimated its size around 240 BC. The myth was popularised in the 1800s.

myths.claim: Einstein failed maths at school
myths.receipt: Einstein was excellent at maths and had taught himself calculus by about 15. The myth likely came from a misread Swiss grading scale.

myths.claim: Summer happens because Earth is closer to the Sun
myths.receipt: Seasons come from Earth's tilt of about 23.4 degrees. Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January, during northern winter.

myths.claim: There's no gravity in space
myths.receipt: On the International Space Station gravity is still about 90 percent as strong as on the ground. Astronauts float because they are constantly falling around the Earth.

myths.claim: Microwaves make your food radioactive
myths.receipt: Microwaves use non-ionising radiation that just makes water molecules jiggle and heat up. Food does not become radioactive.

myths.claim: You lose most of your body heat through your head
myths.receipt: Your head loses heat roughly in proportion to its surface area, around 10 percent. The myth traces back to an old military test where only the head was uncovered.

myths.claim: Glass is a slow-moving liquid
myths.receipt: Glass is an amorphous solid. Old windows are thicker at the bottom because of how they were made and installed, not because they flowed.

myths.claim: Sharks don't get cancer
myths.receipt: Sharks do get cancer; tumours have been documented in many species. The myth was pushed to sell shark cartilage pills.

myths.claim: Camels store water in their humps
myths.receipt: Camel humps store fat, not water. The fat is an energy reserve for long trips.

myths.claim: Mice love cheese
myths.receipt: Mice prefer sweet foods and grains. If you're setting a trap, peanut butter beats cheese.

myths.claim: Lemmings jump off cliffs in mass suicide
myths.receipt: They don't. The myth was cemented by a 1958 Disney documentary where filmmakers herded lemmings off a cliff themselves.

myths.claim: Thomas Edison invented the light bulb
myths.receipt: Incandescent lamps existed for decades before Edison. He made a practical long-lasting bulb and a system to power it, while Joseph Swan was working on the same thing in England.

myths.claim: Humans evolved from chimpanzees
myths.receipt: Humans and chimps share a common ancestor that lived roughly 6 to 7 million years ago. Chimps are cousins, not grandparents.

myths.claim: Fortune cookies are a Chinese tradition
myths.receipt: Fortune cookies were popularised in California in the early 1900s, most likely by Japanese immigrants. They're rare in China.

myths.claim: Marie Antoinette said 'let them eat cake'
myths.receipt: There's no evidence she said it. Rousseau wrote the line about 'a great princess' when Marie Antoinette was still a child in Austria.

myths.claim: Toilets flush the other way in the southern hemisphere
myths.receipt: The Coriolis effect is far too weak to steer a sink or toilet. The shape of the bowl and how the water enters decide the spin.

myths.claim: Carrying a credit card balance boosts your credit score
myths.receipt: Paying your full balance every month is just as good for your score, and you skip the interest. Carrying a balance only costs you money.

myths.claim: Checking your own credit score lowers it
myths.receipt: Checking your own score is a soft inquiry and does not affect it. Only hard inquiries, like applying for credit, can.

myths.claim: Moving into a higher tax bracket means all your income gets taxed more
myths.receipt: Income tax is marginal: only the money above each threshold is taxed at the higher rate. A raise can't make you take home less from income tax alone.

myths.claim: You need a lot of money to start investing
myths.receipt: Many brokers offer fractional shares and index funds with tiny minimums. Time in the market matters more than starting big.

myths.claim: Paper money is made of paper
myths.receipt: US dollar bills are about 75 percent cotton and 25 percent linen, and many countries now use plastic polymer notes.

myths.claim: Incognito mode makes you anonymous online
myths.receipt: Incognito only stops your browser saving history on your device. Websites, your internet provider and your employer's network can still see what you do.

myths.claim: Macs can't get viruses
myths.receipt: Macs can get malware. In 2012 the Flashback trojan infected over 600,000 Macs.

myths.claim: More megapixels means better photos
myths.receipt: Sensor size, lens quality and image processing matter more. A big-megapixel tiny sensor can still take mushy photos.

myths.claim: You should fully drain your phone battery before charging
myths.receipt: That was true for old nickel batteries. Modern lithium-ion batteries prefer partial charges, and deep drains wear them faster.

myths.claim: Closing background apps saves battery
myths.receipt: Apple and Google both say force-closing apps doesn't help and can even use more battery when the app has to restart from scratch.

myths.claim: A higher GHz number always means a faster processor
myths.receipt: Clock speed is one factor. Architecture, core count and cache matter so much that a lower-GHz chip can easily be faster.

myths.claim: Columbus was the first European to reach America
myths.receipt: Norse explorers led by Leif Erikson reached North America around the year 1000, nearly 500 years earlier. And millions of people already lived there.

myths.claim: The pyramids were built by slaves
myths.receipt: Archaeologists found villages and tombs of paid, fed workers near Giza. Building the pyramids was organised labour, not slavery.

myths.claim: Witches were burned at the stake in Salem
myths.receipt: Nobody was burned in Salem. Nineteen people were hanged and one man was crushed with stones.

myths.claim: The iron maiden was a medieval torture device
myths.receipt: There's no solid evidence iron maidens existed in the Middle Ages. Most known examples were assembled in the 1800s for museums and shows.

myths.claim: Walt Disney was cryogenically frozen
myths.receipt: Walt Disney was cremated in 1966. The frozen-head story is pure urban legend.

myths.claim: Sitting too close to the TV ruins your eyes
myths.receipt: There's no evidence it causes lasting damage. The myth took off after some 1960s TVs leaked radiation and were recalled; modern screens don't.

myths.claim: Swallowed gum stays in your stomach for seven years
myths.receipt: Your body can't digest gum base, but it moves through and out like other indigestible stuff, usually within days.

myths.claim: People are either left-brained or right-brained
myths.receipt: A University of Utah study of over 1,000 brain scans found no evidence that people use one side of the brain more than the other.

myths.claim: Coffee stunts your growth
myths.receipt: There's no evidence coffee affects height. The idea was boosted by 1900s ads for a caffeine-free coffee substitute.

myths.claim: Bananas grow on trees
myths.receipt: The banana plant is a giant herb. Its 'trunk' is tightly rolled leaves, not wood.

myths.claim: Strawberries are berries
myths.receipt: Botanically, strawberries aren't berries, but bananas, grapes and even avocados are.

myths.claim: Peanuts are nuts
myths.receipt: Peanuts are legumes, like beans and lentils. They grow underground in pods.

myths.claim: Diamonds are made from coal
myths.receipt: Most diamonds formed deep in the mantle, over 150 km down, often before land plants, the source of coal, even existed.

myths.claim: The Sun is yellow
myths.receipt: Sunlight is basically white. It looks yellow from the ground because the atmosphere scatters blue light.

myths.claim: Mercury is the hottest planet because it's closest to the Sun
myths.receipt: Venus is hotter, around 465 degrees Celsius, because its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat.

myths.claim: Black holes suck everything in like cosmic vacuum cleaners
myths.receipt: From far away a black hole pulls like any object of the same mass. If the Sun became a black hole of equal mass, Earth's orbit wouldn't change.

myths.claim: NASA spent millions on a space pen while Russia used a pencil
myths.receipt: The Fisher Space Pen was developed privately, and both NASA and the Soviets bought it. Pencils shed flammable graphite and broken tips in zero gravity.

myths.claim: The Moon has a permanent dark side
myths.receipt: The far side gets just as much sunlight. It's only hidden from us because the Moon is tidally locked.

myths.claim: You can hear the ocean in a seashell
myths.receipt: You're hearing surrounding noise echoing inside the shell. A cup does the same trick.

myths.claim: Owls can turn their heads all the way around
myths.receipt: Owls can rotate their heads about 270 degrees, thanks to extra neck bones and special blood vessels. Not 360.

myths.claim: Porcupines shoot their quills
myths.receipt: They can't shoot them. The quills detach easily when something touches them.

myths.claim: Cut an earthworm in half and you get two worms
myths.receipt: Usually you just get one injured worm or none. Some species can regrow a lost tail end, not a whole new worm.

myths.claim: One dog year equals seven human years
myths.receipt: Dogs age fast early on. Vets estimate a dog's first year is roughly 15 human years, the second about 9, then around 4 to 5 per year.

myths.claim: House flies only live 24 hours
myths.receipt: House flies usually live around two to four weeks. The one-day thing is closer to adult mayflies.

myths.claim: Hippo milk is pink
myths.receipt: Hippo milk isn't pink. The myth mixed up hippos' reddish skin secretion, sometimes called blood sweat, with their milk.

myths.claim: Koalas are bears
myths.receipt: Koalas are marsupials. They carry their babies in a pouch, like kangaroos.

myths.claim: Killer whales are whales
myths.receipt: Orcas are the largest members of the dolphin family.

myths.claim: All sharks die if they stop swimming
myths.receipt: Some sharks need to keep moving to breathe, but many, like nurse sharks, can pump water over their gills while resting.

myths.claim: You have ten times more bacteria cells than human cells
myths.receipt: A 2016 study revised that to roughly one to one. The ten-to-one number came from a rough 1970s estimate.

myths.claim: The Sahara is the largest desert
myths.receipt: Antarctica is the largest desert. A desert is defined by low precipitation, not heat.

myths.claim: Rubber tyres protect you from lightning in a car
myths.receipt: It's the car's metal body that protects you, by carrying the current around you. A few centimetres of rubber won't stop lightning.

myths.claim: Gold always goes up in value
myths.receipt: Gold peaked around 850 dollars an ounce in 1980 and didn't get back there in nominal terms until 2008. It can drop for decades.

myths.claim: Reading in dim light ruins your eyesight
myths.receipt: It can tire your eyes for a while, but eye doctors say it doesn't cause permanent damage.

myths.claim: Tomatoes are vegetables
myths.receipt: Botanically, tomatoes are fruit. In 1893 the US Supreme Court ruled them vegetables, for tax purposes.
